newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal's govt faces tough wage talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal's govt faces tough wage talks.

text.p: The Portuguese government faced a tough round of negotiations with public sector unions on Monday as it sought to put into place the final piece in its strategy to gain entry to the European Union's planned single currency.

The minority Socialist administration of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has repeatedly warned that it has little room for manoeuvre on wages if it is to meet stiff targets for the budget deficit and inflation next year.
The two sides were meeting on Monday in a bid to narrow a wide gap between what the government says it can afford and what unions, led by the Communist-dominated Common Front, want.

A spokesman told Reuters on Monday that the government was prepared to raise its wage offer to the country's some 500,000 public sector employees to 2.75 percent, from the 2.6 percent already spurned by labour leaders.
Unions are demanding rises of at least 3.5 percent with the Common Front threatening strike action if the government does not boost its offer significantly.
But economists say that the government, which in its 14 months in office has always opted for negotiation over confrontation on important issues, has little option this time but to take a tough line.

They say three percent would be the upper limit for the public sector, whose wage deals set the pace for increases throughout the economy, without jeopardising economic goals, particularly for inflation.
"The maximum that the government could accept would be three percent," said Isabel Costa of Banco Finantia in Lisbon.

The government, which has made Portugal's inclusion in the vanguard of countries launching Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999 its top policy priority, is already guaranteed parliamentary support for a deficit-cutting budget for 1997.
The budget, which should be approved by parliament in a vote this Wednesday or Thursday, predicts a deficit of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), inside the three percent EMU ceiling.

The Socialists are four seats short of an outright majority in parliament, but the economic plan became certain to pass after the small, right-wing Popular Party agreed that its 15 representatives would abstain.
However with a question mark still hanging over the country's performance on inflation, the government had no option but to dig in its heels over wages, economists said.
Price rises are running at just over three percent but the government needed to get the rate down to some 2.5 percent next year to be sure of passing the EMU test.
If unions held out for increases above three percent, then the government could eventually suspend the talks and impose a wage rise, economists said.
"The priority is to control inflation. I think the government will be tough," said Costa.
